items.followUp: Define an ionic bond and give one example.

rubric.why: The definition must state that one atom supplies a lone pair of electrons.
rubric.description: Identifies donation of a lone pair by one atom.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for stating that one atom donates/provides a lone pair to form the bond.

rubric.why: A coordinate covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons, with both electrons supplied by one atom.
rubric.description: Explains that the donated pair is shared between the atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the pair is shared or identifying the bond as coordinate covalent.

rubric.why: An example demonstrates a coordinate covalent bond.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct example, such as NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺ or CO.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by one atom.
After donation, the electron pair is shared between the donor atom and the other atom.
Examples include NH₄⁺ (ammonium ion), H₃O⁺ (hydronium ion) and CO (carbon monoxide).

items.followUp: Define boiling point and state one factor that affects it.

rubric.why: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by vapour in equilibrium with its liquid.
rubric.description: Defines vapour pressure as the pressure of vapour above a liquid at equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the vapour's pressure and its equilibrium with the liquid.

rubric.why: Vapour pressure increases as temperature increases.
rubric.description: States the effect of temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing temperature increases vapour pressure.

rubric.why: The nature of the liquid, including its intermolecular forces or volatility, affects vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Identifies the nature or volatility of the liquid as a factor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the liquid's nature, volatility or intermolecular forces.

rubric.why: Weaker intermolecular forces allow molecules to escape more readily, giving a higher vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Explains how the liquid's nature affects vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking weaker forces or greater volatility with higher vapour pressure (or stronger forces with lower vapour pressure).

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour above a liquid when the vapour and liquid are in dynamic equilibrium in a closed container.
It depends on temperature: increasing the temperature increases vapour pressure.
It also depends on the nature of the liquid and the strength of its intermolecular forces.
A more volatile liquid, with weaker intermolecular forces, has a higher vapour pressure at the same temperature.

items.followUp: Calculate the molarity of a solution prepared by dissolving 5.85 g of NaCl to make 500 cm³ of solution.

rubric.why: Molarity is calculated as the number of moles of solute divided by solution volume in dm³.
rubric.description: Chooses the correct molarity formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for writing M = n/V.

rubric.why: The molar mass of Na₂SO₄ is 142 g mol⁻¹, giving 0.200 mol from 28.4 g.
rubric.description: Finds the molar mass and amount of sodium sulfate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for obtaining 0.200 mol (using molar mass 142 g mol⁻¹).

rubric.why: The solution volume must be converted before using the formula.
rubric.description: Converts the solution volume correctly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for converting 400 cm³ to 0.400 dm³ or 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³.

rubric.why: The calculated concentration is 0.50 mol dm⁻³, equivalent to 500 mol m⁻³.
rubric.description: Gives the correct molarity with a unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct final concentration and unit.

modelAnswer: Given: mass of Na₂SO₄ = 28.4 g = 0.0284 kg; volume of solution = 400 cm³ = 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³.
Molar mass of Na₂SO₄ = (2 × 23) + 32 + (4 × 16) = 142 g mol⁻¹ = 0.142 kg mol⁻¹.
Formula: number of moles, n = mass ÷ molar mass.
Formula: molarity, M = n ÷ volume of solution.
Therefore, molarity = 500 mol m⁻³ = 0.500 mol dm⁻³ (0.500 M).

items.followUp: Write the empirical formula of hydrogen peroxide and carbon dioxide.

rubric.why: The empirical formula of glucose is the simplest whole-number ratio of its atoms.
rubric.description: Writes the empirical formula of glucose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for CH₂O.

rubric.why: Silica has a silicon-to-oxygen ratio of 1:2.
rubric.description: Writes the empirical formula of silica.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for SiO₂.

modelAnswer: Empirical formula of glucose = CH₂O.
Empirical formula of silica = SiO₂.

items.followUp: What is Avogadro's number? How many molecules are present in one mole of water?

rubric.why: A mole is the amount of substance containing Avogadro's number of elementary entities.
rubric.description: Defines a mole using Avogadro's number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles/entities.

rubric.why: A correct example applies the mole quantity to a specified substance and its particles.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of one mole.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example, such as one mole of carbon containing 6.02 × 10²³ atoms, or one mole of water containing 6.02 × 10²³ molecules.

modelAnswer: A mole is the amount of a substance that contains 6.02 × 10²³ elementary entities (atoms, molecules or ions).
For example, 1 mol of carbon contains 6.02 × 10²³ carbon atoms.

items.followUp: Define a compound and name one compound that is liquid at room temperature.

rubric.why: An element is a pure substance made of one kind of atom.
rubric.description: Defines an element.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an element consists of only one kind of atom.

rubric.why: Mercury and bromine are elements that are liquid at room temperature.
rubric.description: Names an element that is liquid at room temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming mercury or bromine.

modelAnswer: An element is a pure substance consisting of only one kind of atom.
Mercury and bromine are elements that occur in the liquid state at room temperature.

items.followUp: Describe Rutherford's gold-foil experiment and state what it showed about the atom.

rubric.why: Rutherford directed alpha particles at a thin metal foil and observed their scattering.
rubric.description: Describes the alpha-particle scattering experiment.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that alpha particles were directed at thin gold foil (or a thin foil) and their paths were observed.

rubric.why: The scattering results led Rutherford to infer a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus and mostly empty space in the atom.
rubric.description: States the conclusion about the nucleus or atomic structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for concluding that the atom has a small, dense, positive nucleus and is mostly empty space.

modelAnswer: Rutherford directed a beam of alpha particles at a very thin gold foil and observed their paths on a fluorescent screen.
Most particles passed straight through, some were deflected, and a very few bounced back.
He concluded that most of an atom is empty space and that its positive charge and most of its mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus.

items.followUp: State the modern periodic law and name the scientist who proposed it.

rubric.why: The modern periodic law relates the periodic properties of elements to their atomic numbers.
rubric.description: States the modern periodic law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.

rubric.why: Henry Moseley put forward the modern periodic law.
rubric.description: Names the scientist who proposed the law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Henry Moseley.

modelAnswer: Modern periodic law: The properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.
This law was put forward by Henry Moseley.
